title: My Pump.fun bot performs well on PAPER but badly LIVE — is ~500ms already too slow?
author: Competitive_Ant_9650
selftext:
I’ve been building an ultra-early Pump.fun trading bot.  
The basic flow is:  
CREATE → 50–160ms micro-flow check → BUY → monitor momentum → exit on the first meaningful drop / no-momentum.  
I’m using Helius + PumpPortal + Pump.fun.  
On PAPER some versions perform surprisingly well, but LIVE the results are much worse. My real BUY landing time is often around 400–600ms.  
I’m trying to understand whether the main problem is execution latency or if the strategy itself has no real edge.  
Has anyone tested something similar?  
Is 400–600ms already too slow for very early Pump.fun entries?  
Are flow acceleration / flow purity actually useful before entry?  
Does a FIRST-DROP exit make sense this early?  
How do you simulate realistic PAPER fills without accidentally creating fake profitability?  
I’m more interested in real execution data than backtest-only results.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: 500ms is not your main problem, the paper fill model is. on very early pump.fun entries the token you bought on paper at the create price got bought live by everyone else a couple hundred ms before you, so your real entry sits several steps worse up the bonding curve and your first-drop exit fires against a worse base. to make paper honest: only count a paper fill if a real transaction at or worse than your price landed after your order timestamp, and take that transaction's price as your fill, not the price you saw. then log your live entries against the paper entries for the same tokens. a constant gap means latency, a gap that grows with how good the paper trade looked means the idea itself. first-drop exits that early are mostly noise, one big wallet selling looks identical to the top. I built Quantradin for exactly the fill-honesty side, quantradin.com, costs nothing and stays on paper, but it is US stocks and options only so no help on solana. the rule above ports anywhere.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
Thanks, this is useful. One thing I want to clarify: for an ultra-early Pump.fun strategy, how would you implement the “honest” paper fill in practice?  
Would you replay the actual on-chain trades after my simulated order timestamp and use the first trade at or worse than my executable price as the fill?  
Also, how would you model the SELL side? My strategy enters very early and tries to exit on the first meaningful loss of momentum/drop. Should the paper exit also wait for a real subsequent transaction that proves my sell could have filled at that price?  
I have LIVE data with roughly 400–600ms landing times, so I can compare identical tokens PAPER vs LIVE. What metrics would you log to separate:  
latency/execution disadvantage,  
bonding-curve/slippage disadvantage,  
a genuinely bad entry/exit signal?  
And if first-drop is mostly noise this early, what would you measure instead to distinguish a temporary large-wallet sell from an actual momentum breakdown?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yes, replay, with one tweak: add your measured latency to the order timestamp before you start scanning, then take the first trade at or worse than your price. same rule on the sell side, first trade at or below your ask after signal plus latency. expect the exit to eat more than the entry did.

comments.author: LipTicklers
comments.body: Also needs slippage and fees which are the main things that eat this alive

comments.author: No_Bit_3377
comments.body: Could you clarify whether the 50–160 ms range includes the time your system spends checking the condition and sending the order? It isn't entirely clear what exactly is included in this time interval. If this represents your system's processing time—specifically condition capture/verification, triggering, order generation, and transmission—then that is a very long time. Your system should operate in the microsecond range internally; only then should you look into optimizing network latency.

comments.author: That-Unit7948
comments.body:
Your 400–600ms live landing time is exactly the part I’d isolate before changing the strategy itself.

We run a staked/SWQoS transaction path from Frankfurt specifically for this kind of workload. If you want, you can test the same bot side by side for 5 days and compare actual landing time / landed slot against your current Helius/PumpPortal path.

If you send me your average TPS, peak burst and current sending path, I can tell you what we’d provision.
